newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour says its planned windfall tax is legal.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour says its planned windfall tax is legal.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party says it has won legal assurances that its proposed tax on the profits of privatised utilities is legal and could not be overturned by courts in Britain or in Europe.

Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, is due to publish the details on Thursday ahead of a speech detailing how he plans to use the proceeds of the "windfall" tax to provide jobs for 250,000 unemployed under-25-year-olds.

Lawyer and judge Michael Beloff said in the eight-page legal opinion or report: "In our view...the windfall tax could not even attract a challenge under domestic law (and it) should not attract a challenge under EC law.
"But, if it did, such challenge would fail (and the tax) would withstand any challenge which may be made under the European Court of Human Rights."

Prime Minister John Major, seizing on media reports that Labour's proposed windfall tax could be challenged in the courts by the companies affected, had challenged Brown to prove his plans were legal.
The windfall tax is the centrepiece of the interim budget that Brown plans to unveil within weeks if Labour wins the election now less that three months away.

With Brown committed to leaving income tax rates and spending plans unchanged, it is the only revenue-raising commitment he has made and is crucial to Labour's vow to make a difference after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Labour sources have suggested the tax could raise five to 10 billion pounds ($eight billion to $16.5 billion).

Labour has not specified which firms will be subject to the tax, designed to soak up what Labour considers are excess profits made by companies which held a monopoly position when privatised. It has said it will consult with utility regulators and interested parties before ruling.
Beloff's report said the introduction of the tax by parliamentary legislation would make it immune to challenge in British courts.
In European courts, it said., the starting point was that direct taxation was a matter for member states.
Since there would be no discrimination between British nationals and nationals of other EU states, there was no breach of the key principle of free movement, it said.

And since it would in principle apply to every privatised utility of a particular kind, courts would not be able to argue that the tax was a state aid on the grounds that it could have been -- but was not -- imposed on other companies.

"If a challenge to the windfall tax were brought in a UK court based on EC law, there is no prospect, in our view, of the court granting an interim injunction to restrain implementation of the tax pending resolution of the dispute," Beloff concluded.

He said there would also be no basis for a challenge in the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg as there was a fair balance between the interests of the general public and the interests of any affected companies.
